papers.title: Finely tuned DDA-PASEF-based immunopeptidomics workflow enhances HLA class I coverage
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based immunopeptidomics is essential for the direct identification of HLA-presented peptides, but its application to low-input and clinical samples remains challenging. In this study, we present an optimized DDA-PASEF-based workflow to improve HLA class I peptide coverage. First, we optimized a magnetic bead-based sample preparation protocol to support analysis from reduced starting material and increase compatibility with automation. We then evaluated LC gradient length and column dimensions to define complementary configurations for high-throughput and high-coverage analysis. For MS acquisition, we fine-tuned key parameters, including ion accumulation time, number of PASEF scans, ion mobility range, and polygon filtering, to improve sensitivity while maintaining a suitable cycle time and limiting pre-CID truncations. The customized polygon filter improved the detection of singly charged HLA class I peptides, thereby broadening the identified immunopeptide repertoire. Finally, TIMS2Rescore was integrated to improve confidence in peptide identification. Overall, this optimized workflow improves HLA class I immunopeptide coverage across different sample types, even from low injected sample amounts, supporting its future applicability to clinically relevant samples.

papers.title: Paired-probe chemoproteomic strategy enables global site-resolved quantification of lysine redox states
papers.abstract: Site-specific quantification of lysine (Lys) redox states remains unexplored, as current approaches identify only a limited number of modification sites without determining their stoichiometry. Allysine, an oxidized form of Lys, provides a model posttranslational modification (PTM) for addressing this challenge by requiring selective enrichment and site-specific stoichiometric quantification. Here, we developed a quantitative chemoproteomic platform for paired redox-state isotopic stoichiometry mapping of lysine, termed PRISM-Lys. We used an Am-alkyne probe for allysine enrichment by reductive amination and developed a complementary Ald-alkyne probe to label Lys, with identical reactions generating the same chemical product. Coupling this paired-probe strategy with a quantitative chemoproteomic workflow enables global site-resolved quantification and stoichiometric analysis of Lys redox states across cells and tissues. Applied to ferroptosis, PRISM-Lys revealed bidirectional, site-selective remodeling of Lys oxidation events associated with ferroptotic progression. Together, PRISM-Lys establishes a paired-chemistry framework for global, site-resolved quantification of Lys redox states, providing a new quantitative perspective for investigating protein oxidation in biological systems.

papers.title: Enhancers Silence Coupled-coding RNAs in Animals
papers.abstract: The exact working mechanism and biogenesis of regulatory non-coding RNAs (rncRNAs), including enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), piRNAs, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), transposons, and other non-coding RNAs, remain enigmatic. Conversely, the unique transcriptional regulation mechanism that differentiates animals from simple unicellular organisms remains elusive in life sciences. We find that regulatory non-coding genes are independent transcription units marked with arginine methylation of nucleosomes within their gene bodies, which is regulated by JMJD5. Enhancer RNAs are similar to those of other regulatory RNAs in targeting the 3-prime UTRs of coupled coding RNAs. All regulatory RNA genes share transcription factors with their target coding genes, both of which are regulated by promoter-proximal RNA Polymerase II pausing and may control the development of animals. Temporal and spatial coding genes and regulatory non-coding genes are intrinsically coupled in animals.

papers.title: The intrinsically disordered N-terminal region of eIF5B nucleates RNA-driven phase separation
papers.abstract: Recently, we found that eukaryotic Initiation Factor 5B (eIF5B) forms cytoplasmic puncta under conditions of cellular stress and that the puncta formation drives an increase in alternative translation initiation. The formation of these puncta depends on the intrinsically disordered N-terminal region of eIF5B (eIF5B-NTR). To address the driving force behind this observation, we reconstituted a purified, binary, in vitro system to study the phase separation potential of the eIF5B-NTR. Utilizing this system, we show that eIF5B-NTR forms RNA-driven condensates at physiological concentrations. Furthermore, we defined the properties of the eIF5B condensates and the amino acid sequence requirements of this polypeptide to form complex liquid-liquid condensates. Truncation mapping identified a central arginine-rich core (residues ~200-400) that drives condensation but forms nearly static droplets in the absence of the rest of the polypeptide. Finally, we tested this model in cells to determine if the in vitro observations apply to the complex cellular environment.

papers.title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
papers.abstract: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.

papers.title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
papers.abstract: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment. The scalability of these structures depends on how strongly they deplete monomers from a shared pool, and tuning the disassembly rate is sufficient to shift their scaling regime. Scaling principles also hold for multiple competing structures, with greater competition imposing stronger constraints on the monomer pool. Together, these results establish a mechanistic framework in which a structure's capacity to adapt is set by how much it draws down shared resources as it grows, a principle that may extend to other intracellular structures that scale with the cells that build them.

papers.title: RNA accessibility sequencing reveals transcriptome-wide RBP binding and RNA structure
papers.abstract: We introduce RAD-seq (RNA Accessibility via Deamination sequencing), a simple and scalable method that quantifies RNA accessibility by protein binding in vivo. RAD-seq uses TadA8.20-mediated adenosine deamination to report the local exposure of each adenosine to its molecular environment, integrating the combined effects of base pairing, RNA folding, and RNA-binding protein (RBP) occupancy in a single experiment. RAD-seq profiles recapitulate known structural signatures, reveal high-resolution RBP footprints, report on the influence of RNA modifications, and capture dynamic remodeling of RNA accessibility during oxidative and heat-shock stress. By integrating RAD-seq with RNA Bind-n-Seq motifs, we detected local enrichment of the RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methyltransferase recruiter TRA2A following knockdown of the exon junction anchor protein EIF4A3, revealing a potential mechanism that links RNA accessibility to enhanced TRA2A recruitment and m6A deposition. Extending this framework, we introduce an unsupervised statistical model that combines RAD-seq with motif priors to infer binding landscapes for multiple RBPs, reproducing the information from numerous CLIP-seq datasets from a single RAD-seq experiment. These results indicate RAD-seq as a generalizable approach for joint profiling of RNA structure and protein occupancy, defining enzymatic RNA accessibility as a new dimension to investigate regulatory elements on RNA.

papers.title: Engineering morphology of tetrasulfide-incorporated mesoporous silica nanoparticles for enhanced mRNA delivery
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the most studied nanocarrier for mRNA delivery, yet their broader application remains limited due to suboptimal cellular uptake, low efficacy in mRNA delivery, and poor stability. In this study, we report a novel tetrasulfide-incorporated virus-like porous silica (VLPSi) nanoparticle as a safe and efficient platform to enhance LNP-mediated mRNA delivery. By systematically tuning the synthesis parameters, a series of nanoparticles with distinct morphologies and architectures were obtained, enabling the study of how tetrasulfide and particle morphology affect mRNA delivery. The performance of VLPSi was optimized by evaluating cellular uptake, cytotoxicity, and transfection performance with different lipid and mRNA payloads across multiple cell types. The results showed that increasing the length and number of spikes on the VLPSi surface significantly improved cellular uptake efficiency and subsequent mRNA expression. Mechanistically, the enhanced delivery arose from the combined effect from the nanospikes and intracellular tetrasulfide degradation. Furthermore, the nanoparticles significantly enhanced the stability of mRNA. Overall, these findings establish a structure-function relationship between virus-like topography, biodegradable silica chemistry, and mRNA delivery. This work provides a structurally tunable, biodegradable, and highly effective bioinspired nanoplatform to enhance mRNA delivery.

papers.title: Actin filament bundling by the Arabidopsis VILLIN4 C-terminus involves the basic segment of the IDR linker and is sensitive to temperature and ionic strength
papers.abstract: Plant villins are ubiquitous proteins involved in F-actin regulation in all plant organs. Villins consist of folded core and headpiece domains connected by an intrinsically disordered linker. In plant villins these linkers include up to 200 amino acid residues, which is substantially larger than their vertebrate counterparts (~40 residues). Moreover, the linkers in most types of plant villins exhibit a distinct charge partitioning pattern: a larger basic N-terminus and a smaller acidic C-terminus. The roles of these distinct, sizable and disordered linkers in plant villins are not well understood and are currently under active scrutiny. Here we demonstrate that the basic portion of the linker in Arabidopsis thaliana VILLIN4 (AtVLN4) is capable of actin filament bundling. These interactions are also affected by the presence of the adjacent headpiece domain and are altered by temperature and levels of potassium ions, major abiotic regulators that influence plant growth. Based on these findings, we propose that the F-actin bundling capacity of the basic segment in AtVLN4 is responsive to environmental changes and is a uniform property in closely related villins due to high sequence homology across multiple species.

papers.title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
papers.abstract: -Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson's disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell's proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic. Inclusions took up whole assemblies, with subunits moving together in 421 of 438 complexes, and the V-ATPase alone was enriched in all three systems. Degradation cargo stayed with the receptors that route it, consistent with sequestration and failed degradation acting together. Neuritic and somatic inclusions differed, the former rich in UBQLN2 and the latter in intermediate filaments. In the cell line, phosphorylated -synuclein was tenfold higher in the inclusion than in the rest of the cell, with about one third of the rise already present before an inclusion was visible. Measured against its host, the composition of an inclusion becomes a readout of how it formed and a source of candidate markers and therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Mapping the sequence determinants of constitutive activity in GPCRs
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) signal not only in response to ligands but also in their absence. This basal, or constitutive, activity has distinct physiological consequences and is the only functional measurement available for orphan receptors. It is also hard to compare receptors because each is reported relative to its own baseline. Here, we measure basal activity on a single scale across the human GPCR family. Pairing a barcoded library of all human GPCRs with a transcriptional cAMP reporter, we scored 901 receptor constructs in one pool experiment. Basal activity forms a continuous distribution, and many of the highest-scoring recipes have prior reports of ligand-independent activity, with orphan being strongly represented. We then exhaustively mutated one of them, GPR161, and measured its effects on protein abundance, surface expression, and cAMP signaling. Of the 528 positions, only 10 specifically alter signaling independent of expression. Constraints on basal signaling are dominated by reepotro biogenesis, which requires multiphenotype scanning to resolve. Together, these datasets place basal activity on a common scale across the GPCR family and provide a template for dissecting it at residue resolution.

papers.title: GNG2-MRAS interaction regulates SHOC2-dependent RAF activation and MAPK signaling
papers.abstract: Dysregulation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway is a hallmark of many human cancers and RASopathies. The SHOC2-MRAS-PP1C; (SMP) holophosphatase complex is a crucial regulatory node of this pathway. It activates the MAPK pathway by dephosphorylating the inhibitory phosphoserine on RAF kinases and thereby relieving RAF autoinhibition. Although GNG2, the {gamma}-subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins, has recently emerged as a negative modulator of MAPK signaling, its molecular mechanism of action remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify GNG2 and its truncated variants as inhibitors of SMP complex assembly by directly targeting MRAS. Using NanoBiT live-cell bioluminescence, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), biolayer interferometry (BLI), and molecular dynamics simulation studies, we demonstrate that full-length GNG2 (residues 1-71aa) and two helical fragments ({Delta}1, residues 1-29aa and {Delta}2, residues 30-71aa) bind MRAS, disrupt SMP complex formation, and therefore prevent RAF dephosphorylation. Expression of the truncated GNG2 variants significantly reduced phosphorylation of ERK in cells, consistent with inhibition of pathway activation. Furthermore, a short peptide synthesized from the GNG2 {Delta}2 sequence effectively disrupted SMP complex formation in both purified protein systems and live cells and potently attenuated MAPK signaling. Molecular dynamics simulation studies revealed that GNG2 variants engage with the Switch I/II regions of MRAS, sterically interfering with SHOC2-PP1C association. Together, these findings establish GNG2 as a direct regulator of SMP complex assembly and demonstrate that GNG2-derived peptides represent a promising strategy for disrupting SHOC2-MRAS interactions and suppressing MAPK signaling in RAS/RAF-driven pathologies.

papers.title: Functional Reconstitution of Human OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 in Proteoliposomes: Effect of Bicarbonate Gradients and Substrate-specific Stimulation on Transport
papers.abstract: The hepatic organic anion transporting polypeptides OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 are critical for the clearance of widely prescribed drugs, hepatotoxins, and endogenous metabolites. However, the thermodynamic driving force governing their transport has remained a subject of debate due to the complexity of cellular models. Here, we report a defined, reconstituted proteoliposome system to study the transport kinetics of isolated human OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. Through direct functional assays, real-time counter-ion tracking, and a novel ABCG2-OATP1B1 functional co-reconstitution, we identify an outwardly directed bicarbonate gradient as a thermodynamic driving force for concentrative substrate uptake. In contrast we find no evidence for the proposed role of reduced glutathione efflux as a possible driving force. Targeted mutagenesis experiments revealed that the conserved TM3 residue His115 is needed to couple the bicarbonate gradient to concentrative substrate uptake, mechanistically linking substrate antiport to local pH-sensitive bicarbonate processing. We also investigated the substrate-specific stimulatory effect of the green tea catechin epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) on OATP1B3 transport, confirming that this effect is intrinsic to OATP1B3, substrate specific, and does not need the involvement of other cellular proteins. Our findings define the energetic basis of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 hepatic xenobiotic clearance.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structures of Cereibacter sphaeroides ferrochelatase reveal an oligomeric state that occludes the substrate-binding site
papers.abstract: Protoporphyrin IX (PPIX) is the last shared intermediate of heme and (bacterio)chlorophyll ((B)Chl) biosynthesis. Insertion of iron into PPIX by the PPIX ferrochelatase (FeCh) PpfC produces heme, whereas magnesium insertion by magnesium chelatase (MgCh) initiates (B)Chl synthesis. Chlorophototrophic organisms must regulate this biosynthetic node to ensure the correct flux of PPIX to each of these crucial tetrapyrrole products, presenting a particularly acute problem for the facultative bacterium Cereibacter (previously Rhodobacter) sphaeroides, which can switch between chemotrophic (respiratory) and phototrophic (photosynthetic) growth modes. To elucidate the structural basis for the catalytic and regulatory functions of C. sphaeroides FeCh (PpfCCs), we used cryogenic electron microscopy to determine its structure, to our knowledge the first such information for a Gram-negative or phototrophic organism. We determined the 2.6 [A] structure of an active site mutant of PpfCCs, which forms a dimer with a monomer-to-monomer interface that coordinates two hemes. We also determined a 2.5 [A] structure of the wild-type enzyme, in which two dimers interact in a homotetrameric arrangement that occludes PPIX binding at the active site of each monomer. We propose that the PpfCCs dimer likely docks onto the inner membrane in a manner analogous to the human enzyme, whereas the tetramer represents a transiently inactive state whereby the hydrophobic lips and active site are both occluded. These novel oligomerization states of FeCh may have evolved to influence the flux of tetrapyrroles through the heme/BChl branchpoint in purple bacteria.

papers.title: Mapping bacterial bile amidation across the bile salt hydrolase family
papers.abstract: Evaluating enzyme activity and specificity in complex microbiomes is challenging. The recent discovery that bacterial bile salt hydrolases (BSHs) also function as transaminases in the human gut microbiome highlights what remains to be disentangled, even within one of the most extensively studied microbiomes. BSHs as transaminases can conjugate bile acids with bioavailable amines to produce bacterial bile amidates (BBAs). The implications of BBAs for human health are rapidly evolving, but our understanding of which BSHs produce which specific BBAs remains limited. Here, we connect BSH sequence and function by evaluating the transaminase activities of 115 BSHs and reveal distinct amine specificities using molecular networking. Additionally, we identify enzymatically generated BBAs distributed across life-stage, tissue-, and disease-specific human samples by mining public metabolomics repositories, highlighting the previously unrecognized catalytic diversity of BSHs and their potential relevance to human health.

papers.title: Molecular insights into the regulation of coenzyme selection in NADP-specific glutamate dehydrogenase from Saccharomyces cerevisiae
papers.abstract: Coenzyme specificity is one of the crucial aspects of the functional regulations in enzymes. Understanding the molecular basis of coenzyme specificity in glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is highly essential as this is the only enzyme that fulfils various physiological demands in terms of energy production and/or nitrogen assimilation via its strict functional regulation by connecting carbon and nitrogen metabolic cycles in every living organism. We have studied S. cerevisiae GDH3 (ScGDH3), as a model system for NADP-specific fungal GDHs. K272R and S250E mutants of ScGDH3 exhibited remarkable alteration in coenzyme specificity, with 15-55-fold and 3-14-fold more preference towards non-specific coenzymes [NAD(H)], respectively. S250E exhibited higher NADH affinity (~ 1.3-fold) than that of towards NADPH. K272R showed ~ 10-fold increased coenzyme affinity (1/KM) and binding affinity (1/kd) towards NADH, compared to the wild type enzyme (ScGDH3-WT). We solved the crystal structure of ScGDH3-K272R complexed with NADP+ at 2.50 [A] resolution with a unique oligomeric arrangement having two distinct subunit conformations (''open'' and ''super-closed'') and it is the first structure of a GDH from S. cerevisiae. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide insights into NADH binding and its increased affinity to ScGDH3-K272R. Further structure-based sequence analyses unravelled that a lysine and an arginine are naturally preferred residues for providing NADP(H) and NAD(H) specificity, respectively for various amino acid dehydrogenases. Taken together biochemical and structural data, our study successfully illustrates the evolutionary conserved mechanism of coenzyme related regulation in fungal and other GDHs; as well as amino acid dehydrogenases.

papers.title: Structural Basis for Inhibition of Human Anion Transporter SLC26A6/PAT-1
papers.abstract: PAT-1, encoded by the gene SLC26A6, is an exchanger of small organic and inorganic anions including oxalate and chloride in the kidney and the intestines. PAT-1 dysfunction is implicated in nephrolithiasis and hyperoxaluria, and its modulation is a potential therapeutic strategy to treat cystic fibrosis. PAT-1 has two small molecule inhibitors: DIDS, a non-specific anion exchanger inhibitor; and PAT1inh-B01 which is highly specific to PAT-1. In this study, we report high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of the human PAT-1 homodimer in complex with these inhibitors to reveal their different inhibition mechanisms. These structures also uncover the complex interactions between the transmembrane, STAS and N-terminal domains, with implications on its ion exchange function. Hence, this study provides mechanistic insight into PAT-1 molecular function and inhibition, and contributes to our understanding of SLC26 transport mechanisms.

papers.title: Direct Bioconjugations of Diverse Payloads using an Extraordinarily Donor-Promiscuous Flavin Transferase
papers.abstract: Site-specific protein conjugation is a widely used tool in chemical biology research and is the foundation of many biotechnological and biomedical applications. A key enabling technology are repurposed post-translational protein modifying enzymes, where variants with broad donor and acceptor substrate promiscuity were developed into general-purpose bioconjugation platforms. However, direct enzymatic attachment of bulky or structurally diverse payloads is often limited by low reaction efficiencies and difficulties in preparing suitable donors. Consequently, conjugation typically relies on two-step strategies in which an enzyme first installs a bioorthogonal handle on the target protein, followed by chemical attachment of the payload. These enzyme-first, chemistry-second approaches limit chemistry to bioorthogonal reactions that leave a molecular footprint. Here, we introduce direct ADDing, an enzymatic bioconjugation platform based on our discovery of the exceptional donor promiscuity of the flavin transferase ApbE. We show that ApbE accepts a remarkably broad range of donor substrates provided they carry an adenosine diphosphate (ADP) anchor. The prevalence of ADP-containing compounds in nature provides access to diverse building blocks and an extensive biochemical toolbox for donor generation. Exploiting these resources, we demonstrate multiple strategies for preparing compatible donors and achieve direct, site-specific enzymatic conjugation of diverse small molecules, peptides, proteins, and synthetic polymers.

papers.title: A respiratory microdomain links ubiquinone biosynthesis to succinate dehydrogenase in an apicomplexan mitochondrion lacking Complex I
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial complex I (CI) is a major entry point for NADH-derived electrons and an important site of redox regulation in most eukaryotes. However, apicomplexan parasites, including Toxoplasma gondii, lack CI, raising a fundamental question of how mitochondrial respiration is organized in these parasites. Here, we identify a parasite-specific mitochondrial microdomain that physically and functionally couples ubiquinone (UQ) biosynthesis to succinate dehydrogenase (SDH). Using proximity labeling, membrane-based yeast two-hybrid analyses, reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations, and blue native PAGE, we show that UQ biosynthesis proteins associate with parasite-specific SDH subunits and co-migrate as a high-molecular-weight assembly. Knockdown of TgCoq4, a component of the UQ biosynthesis pathway, reduced SDH activity, and adding exogenous UQ to the assay did not restore it, indicating that UQ availability is not sufficient for efficient succinate oxidation. FCCP stimulates malate- and TMPD/ascorbate-supported respiration to maximal capacity but fails to do so with succinate as the substrate. This result, combined with reactive oxygen species (ROS) data, suggests that succinate causes over-reduction of the UQ pool, limiting further electron flow. We also find that CIII associates with the UQ synthesis machinery, suggesting a larger protein assembly. Together, these findings reveal that UQ biosynthesis and electron transport are physically and functionally integrated in T. gondii, defining a previously unrecognized organization of mitochondrial respiration in an organism lacking CI.

papers.title: Human senataxin uses distinct peripheral elements to unwind R-loops and act on RNA polymerase II
papers.abstract: Persistent R-loops and paused or stalled RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) elongation complexes can threaten genome stability. Senataxin (SETX) contributes to R-loop resolution and RNAPII regulation, but their intimate connection during transcription makes the individual contributions of these activities difficult to distinguish in cells. To determine whether these activities rely on the same molecular features, we investigated the structure and biochemical properties of the SETX helicase domain (SETX-HD). Cryo-EM defines the conserved helicase core and RNA-binding channel of SETX-HD, while biochemical analyses identify distinct roles for two peripheral elements: a previously uncharacterised C-terminal RNA-binding domain (CT-RBD) and the prong subdomain. In reconstituted mammalian transcription assays, SETX-HD promotes passage beyond a defined RNAPII pause and elongation-complex dissociation on the same template. The CT-RBD stabilises RNA engagement and is required for efficient R-loop unwinding, whereas its deletion preserves both RNAPII-associated activities. Conversely, replacing the native SETX prong with its fungal Sen1 counterpart preserves R-loop unwinding but impairs both RNAPII outcomes. These reciprocal separation-of-function effects establish that a common SETX-HD RNA-translocation core depends on distinct peripheral elements for R-loop unwinding and action on mammalian RNAPII. This separation provides a direct route to determine how these activities contribute to SETX function in cells.

papers.title: The small ORF (smORF)-encoded polypeptide MIRINE promotes neuronal differentiation in vertebrate brain development
papers.abstract: The vertebrate brain expresses an extensive repertoire of long-noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), an emerging source of small open reading frame (smORF)-encoded polypeptides (SEPs) whose functions remain largely unknown. Using ribosome profiling and proteomics of zebrafish and mouse brain, we identified hundreds of translated smORFs. We characterized MIRINE, a SEP of 83 amino acids conserved across 205 vertebrate species. MIRINE contains a transmembrane domain that targets it to the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles, and is enriched in cortical and hippocampal neurons, with expression rising during neurogenesis. Downregulation of Mirine increased cell proliferation and impaired neuronal maturation in neuroblastoma cells, in mouse primary cortical neurons and cortex, and in the zebrafish forebrain, identifying MIRINE as a regulator of the balance between neuronal proliferation and differentiation. Mechanistically, MIRINE associates with the synaptic-vesicle protein Synaptogyrin-3 and related membrane proteins. Our findings define a conserved, membrane-associated SEP controlling neuronal maturation and illustrate the functional potential of brain SEPs.

papers.title: Uncovering the Multifaceted Role of the Kinetochore Scaffold 1 (KNL1) in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Integrative Bioinformatics Analysis and CRISPR-Cas9 Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by pronounced heterogeneity, chromosomal instability, and limited therapeutic options. Kinetochore scaffold 1 (KNL1), a core mitotic checkpoint component, is implicated in multiple cancers, but its role in HCC remains unclear. Here, we integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses with functional in vitro validation to elucidate the biological and clinical significance of KNL1 in HCC. KNL1 was markedly overexpressed in HCC tumors, particularly those harbouring TP53 mutations, and correlated with increased tumor break load, suggesting a link to structural chromosomal instability. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and hallmark gene set enrichment identified a KNL1-associated G2M checkpoint network, in which KNL1 ranked among the top 10 hub genes. A KNL1-G2M network score, stratified patients into high- and low-score groups, with high scores correlates with poorer overall survival, increased proliferation, and higher chromosomal instability. Immune deconvolution (CIBERSORTx) revealed that high-score tumors were enriched in T-regulatory cells and M0 macrophages, and had elevated TIDE and exclusion scores, indicating potential resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Single-cell RNA-seq confirmed preferential activation of the KNL1-G2M module in malignant hepatocytes and highlighted increased extracellular matrix remodeling and immunomodulatory interactions. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated KNL1 downregulation in HepG2 cells induced modest G2/M arrest, suppressed proliferation, reduced survivin and Bcl2 expression, and produced ultrastructural changes consistent with early apoptosis. Collectively, our results implicate KNL1 and its associated G2/M network in tumor progression-related processes, including chromosomal instability, proliferative activity, and immune modulation in HCC. While further mechanistic and clinical studies are required, KNL1 and its associated network may represent a biologically relevant vulnerability and a potential biomarker of aggressive disease behavior in hepatocellular carcinoma.

papers.title: Selective binders of a cotranslational folding intermediate
papers.abstract: Drug discovery efforts typically target mature, folded proteins, primarily to inhibit their function or induce their degradation. An alternative strategy would be to target incompletely folded states that are transiently populated during protein biogenesis, but whether these states contain druggable pockets was unclear. Here, we used an mRNA display approach to discover cyclic peptides that recognize a nascent polypeptide at an intermediate point during its synthesis on the ribosome. We identified peptides that bind with low-nanomolar affinity to a model nascent protein, {beta}-galactosidase, but do not detectably bind either the fully-folded protein or ribosomes synthesising different sequences. Hydrogen/deuterium exchange-mass spectrometry and cryogenic electron microscopy revealed the molecular basis for selective binding. We found that the nascent chain folds into an -helix against the ribosome surface during ongoing translation, creating a cryptic pocket together with ribosomal proteins uL23 and uL29 that is exploited by the hit peptides. Our results establish proof-of-concept for selective targeting of protein biogenesis intermediates, and provide a platform for future drug development.

papers.title: QC-espresso: Brewing quality in proteomics
papers.abstract: Data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics has become a standard approach for high-throughput proteomics, with DIA-NN emerging as one of the most widely adopted data-analysis platforms. However, despite the detailed information available in DIA-NN output reports, proteomics researchers may lack a streamlined and reproducible approach for assessing acquisition quality, identification consistency, and quantitative reliability across experiments. QC-espresso addresses this need through an automated, report-centered quality-control workflow implemented in R and Quarto. The tool processes a DIA-NN report.parquet file together with the corresponding FASTA database and generates a structured HTML report containing plots, run-level statistics, and exportable summary tables. Application to three experimental datasets allowed the visualization of lower identification depth related to high contaminant content; a chromatographic transition accompanied by altered retention-time and peak-width behavior; and the co-occurrence of systematic mass-error bias with changes in precursor- and protein-level quantitative-quality metrics. QC-espresso can be executed directly in R or through a portable Windows distribution with a graphical launcher, with both modes using the same analytical modules and report-generation workflow. The resulting report provides a consistent record for local inspection and troubleshooting of quality-control metrics within individual DIA proteomics experiments. QC-espresso is freely available at https://github.com/lanfredig/QC-espresso_DIA.

papers.title: Molecular crowding differentially regulates magnetic field-dependent fluorescence, recovery kinetics, and photostability of the magnetosensitive protein MagLOV2
papers.abstract: Macromolecular crowding and solvent composition can alter protein conformation, diffusion, hydration, and cofactor photophysics, yet their influence on magnetically sensitive flavoproteins is poorly understood. We tested seven molecular environments in MagLOV2-overexpressing Escherichia coli lysate using a custom-built, high-intensity magnetofluorescence platform. Five-point concentration series of Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, PEG6000, PEG3350, glycerol, ethylene glycol, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were measured at 22 mT under continuous 6.12 W/cm2 blue-light excitation. Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, and PEG6000 progressively attenuated the negative magnetic field effect (MFE), whereas PEG3350 shifted toward mild enhancement at higher concentrations. Glycerol and ethylene glycol enhanced the negative MFE despite producing the strongest slowing of recovery upon the field being switched off (OFF-recovery), while BSA modestly enhanced MFE and accelerated OFF-recovery. Across 105 treatment cuvettes, the change in MFE was not globally correlated with changes in the OFF-recovery time constant (r = -0.07, p = 0.449). The initial pre-field illumination period revealed a second phenotype: Dextran and Ficoll increased late fluorescence loss, whereas glycerol and BSA were photoprotective. Pre-field fluorescence loss correlated moderately with MFE change across the full dataset (r = 0.474, p = 3.28 x 10-7) but not consistently within crowder classes. These findings show that MagLOV2 spin-dependent magnetofluorescence is shaped by crowder chemistry, polymer size, solvent environment, recovery kinetics, and photostability rather than by a single generic crowding or viscosity mechanism.

papers.title: A RecBCD-like enzyme regulates expression of bacterial defense operons in response to DNA damage
papers.abstract: Bacteria must quickly respond to stress signals including bacteriophage (phage) infection, invasion by mobile genetic elements, and other threats. DNA damage is a stress-signaling nexus in bacteria, initiating global responses such as the SOS response and triggering expression of specific defense and immune pathways through DNA damage-sensing transcriptional regulators. Here we identify a three-protein pathway termed Cerberus that senses dsDNA ends that become available during DNA damage or inhibition of the key DNA repair complex RecBCD, and controls expression of an associated defense/immune operon. The central player in Cerberus is a large peptidase-helicase-nuclease fusion protein, CerC, that is architecturally similar to the RecBC complex itself. Upon DNA damage or RecBCD inhibition, CerC binds and unwinds free DNA ends to allosterically activate its fused HExxH metallopeptidase domain. CerC specifically cleaves the adjacently encoded anti-sigma factor CerB to release its cognate sigma factor CerA, allowing CerA to mediate transcription of a defense/immune operon encoded nearby. Cerberus therefore represents a pathway that has co-opted a key DNA repair machine for DNA damage sensing, and linked that activity to transcriptional control through anti-sigma factor cleavage.

papers.title: MASH-in-a-dish reveals fatty acid-driven itaconate crosstalk between Kupffer cells and hepatocytes
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is characterized by lipid-driven sterile inflammation and fibrosis that leads to liver failure and liver cancer. Metabolites are increasingly recognized as signaling molecules and regulate disease progression through cell-cell crosstalk. To overcome the challenges of studying metabolite crosstalk between different cell types in MASH livers, we developed a novel in vitro MASH model, "MASH-in-a-dish", a Transwell co-culture system of mouse hepatocyte-derived organoids (HepOrgs), Kupffer cells (KCs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) in a chemically defined liver co-culture medium. MASH-in-a-dish models key clinical features of clinical MASH, including steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, inflammation and fibrosis. MASH-in-a-dish allowed for rapid and specific separation of co-cultured HepOrgs, KCs and HSCs, enabling cell type-specific metabolomics and stable-isotope fluxomics analysis. Using MASH-in-a-dish, we identified 19 MASH-associated, cell interaction-responsive metabolites and demonstrated that fatty acids, via the carnitine shuttle, drive KC itaconate production, which aggravated oxidative stress, steatosis, and cell damage in lipid-stressed HepOrgs. Inhibiting itaconate production by KC-specific Acod1 knockout in the MASH-in-a-dish system mitigated hepatocyte damage. Our results show that MASH-in-a-dish is a powerful in vitro platform to study cell-cell interactions in MASH pathogenesis and identify itaconate crosstalk between Kupffer cells and hepatocytes as a novel pathogenic mechanism and a potential therapeutic target in MASH.

papers.title: Heterogeneous primary nucleation determines Aβ42 fibrilstructure.
papers.abstract: The current developments in the field of amyloid fibril structure determination has revealed multiple structures for peptides of identical sequence. This may reflect variations in sample environment or similar nucleation barriers for multiple folds. Here we investigate the influence of aggregating surface and during fibril formation from monomeric amyloid {beta} peptide (A{beta}42). The fibril structures formed in identical solutions in glass vials / bottles and PEGylated polystyrene 96-well plates display very different monomer fold within the fibrils. This is a clear indication of extremely slow homogeneous primary nucleation. Instead, heterogeneous primary nucleation at vessel walls or at the three-line interface between air, water and vessel wall dictate the outcome in each solution, where the initially formed structure is propagated through elongation and secondary nucleation. The results further imply that the conversion towards the thermodynamically stable fibril structure one is slow for A{beta}42.

papers.title: Recognition of the centromere-binding protein Ndc10 by Scm3HJURP directs Cse4CENP-A deposition at native centromeres
papers.abstract: Kinetochores connect centromeres to spindle microtubules, ensuring accurate chromosome segregation. Kinetochore assembly at centromeres depends on deposition of CENP-A, a histone H3 variant. Despite considerable progress, how CENP-A is specifically assembled on native centromeres remains an open question. Centromere-specific assembly of CENP-A occurs spontaneously in a cell-free extract system from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, but with low efficiency, suggesting that one or more factors are limiting. Here, we show Scm3HJURP, a specific chaperone for the centromeric histone Cse4CENP-A, is one such limiting component. The addition of a complex of Scm3, Cse4 and histone H4 strongly stimulates Cse4 assembly in a centromeric DNA sequence- and dose-dependent manner; in addition, improvements in both Cse4 and kinetochore assembly were more prominent in mitotic versus interphase (G1) extracts. Using the complemented cell-free reconstitution system, we show that distinct Scm3 interfaces with Cse4 and with the Ndc10 subunit of the yeast centromere DNA sequence-recognizing CBF3 complex are essential for centromere-specific Cse4 assembly and cell viability. Thus, recognition of Ndc10 directs Scm3-dependent and locus-specific centromeric histone deposition.

papers.title: An Integrated Experimental and Informatics Strategy Enables Large Proteoform Identification in Top-Down Proteomics
papers.abstract: Top-down proteomics enables identification and characterization of intact proteoforms, preserving information on co-occurring sequence variations and post-translational modifications. However, identifying large proteoforms remains challenging due to an exponential decrease in signal-to-noise ratio with increasing molecular weight, interference from coeluting smaller species, unresolved precursor isotopic envelopes, difficulty obtaining informative MS/MS spectra, and limitations of current informatics tools. To address these challenges, here we present an integrated experimental and informatics strategy combining protein separation, data acquisition, precursor mass assignment, and MS/MS interpretation. First, we demonstrate that online two-dimensional liquid chromatography coupling size-exclusion and reversed-phase separations enables facile detection of large proteoforms. We then utilize a precursor mass correction strategy to enable conventional database searching of data-dependent acquisition (DDA) data containing isotopically unresolved precursors. Finally, we use data-independent acquisition (DIA) optimized for large proteins to enhance fragment signal and enable identification through intact-mass-guided candidate discovery and MS/MS validation. Applied to human heart tissue, the integrated strategy identified 703 nonredundant proteoforms from 236 unique proteins, including 65 proteins >30 kDa and 22 proteins >50 kDa, with identifications extending to 223 kDa. This integrated strategy bridges the detection-to-identification gap for large proteins and expands the accessible mass range of discovery top-down proteomics.
